Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-10.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Current advancements in speech processing are bifurcated into two distinct tracks: representation learning (discriminative tasks like recognition) and generative modeling (synthesis tasks like TTS). Predominant pre-training techniques for discriminative tasks, such as masked auto-encoding, tend to compress speech into semantic representations, intentionally discarding acoustic variations like speaker timbre and environmental noise. Conversely, generative models require these exact acoustic details to produce high-fidelity audio. Consequently, researchers currently must train and maintain separate foundation models for understanding and generation, resulting in significant computational overhead and sub-optimal information sharing between the two modalities. There is a lack of a unified framework capable of learning high-quality semantic abstractions while simultaneously retaining the acoustic fidelity required for generation.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that speech representation learning and generative modeling are complementary rather than conflicting objectives. We propose that by designing a unified encoder-decoder architecture trained jointly from scratch, the discriminative objective can guide the model to understand semantic structure, while the generative objective ensures the preservation of fine-grained acoustic details. We believe that a representation encoder, when subjected to both self-distillation (for stability and semantics) and a generative flow-matching objective (for reconstruction), will yield a "super-representation" capable of serving both speech recognition and synthesis tasks without the need for separate foundation models.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)

We propose to develop **UniWav**, a unified pre-training framework that integrates a Transformer-based encoder and decoder into a single end-to-end training pipeline. The methodology focuses on two simultaneous learning signals:

**1. The Representation Encoder (Discriminative Stream)**
We will employ a masked audio modeling approach where the model takes masked surface features (e.g., audio codes or spectrograms) as input. To learn robust semantic representations, we will utilize **self-distillation**.
*   **Mechanism:** The encoder will function as a "student" network attempting to predict pseudo-labels generated by a "teacher" network.
*   **The Teacher:** To avoid collapse and ensure stable targets, the teacher will be a momentum-updated version (Exponential Moving Average) of the student encoder itself.
*   **Online Clustering:** The teacher's outputs will be dynamically clustered into codebooks to provide discrete targets for the student, forcing the encoder to learn structural categorizations of the audio data.

**2. The Generative Decoder (Generative Stream)**
We will attach a decoder designed to reconstruct the original audio from the encoder’s latent representations.
*   **Flow Matching:** Instead of simple reconstruction loss, we will adopt a Flow Matching objective. This involves learning a vector field that transforms a simple prior distribution (noise) into the complex data distribution (speech) over time.
*   **Conditioning:** The decoder will not just take the final output of the encoder. It will be conditioned on a learnable weighted sum of representations from *all* layers of the encoder. This allows the decoder to select the appropriate level of abstraction (low-level acoustic vs. high-level semantic) needed for high-fidelity generation.

**3. Joint Optimization**
The entire system will be trained end-to-end. The total objective will be a weighted combination of the encoder's self-distillation loss and the decoder's flow matching loss. By training from scratch, the encoder is forced to structure its latent space to satisfy both the discrete classification needs of the teacher and the continuous reconstruction needs of the decoder.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Unified Foundation Model:** We expect to demonstrate the feasibility of a single model that competes with specialized state-of-the-art models in both speech recognition (ASR) and text-to-speech (TTS), proving that task-specific pre-training is not strictly necessary.
2.  **Training Efficiency:** By consolidating two training pipelines into one, we aim to significantly reduce the computational overhead and cost associated with developing speech foundation models.
3.  **Versatile Representations:** The approach should yield representations that are semantically rich yet acoustically complete. This is expected to enable novel capabilities in tasks that sit at the intersection of understanding and generation, such as high-quality, low-bitrate speech tokenization and resynthesis.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We designed and executed a series of experiments to validate a unified pre-training framework for speech, capable of handling both representation learning (discriminative) and generation tasks.

*   **Datasets:**
    *   **Pre-training:** LibriLight audiobook corpus (approx. 60,000 hours of untranscribed English speech).
    *   **Fine-tuning & Evaluation:** LibriSpeech corpus.
        *   *Speech Recognition:* Fine-tuned on 960 hours (full) or train-clean-100 (100 hours). Evaluated on test-other.
        *   *Speech Synthesis:* Fine-tuned on LibriSpeech train-clean-100 and train-clean-360. Evaluated on test-clean (3-second enrollment).
        *   *Tokenization:* Trained on LibriSpeech. Evaluated on dev-clean, dev-other, test-clean, and test-other.
    *   **SUPERB Benchmark:** Used for Phoneme Recognition and Speaker Identification tasks.

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **Speech Recognition:** Word Error Rate (WER) and Phoneme Error Rate (PER).
    *   **Speech Synthesis (In-context TTS):**
        *   *ASR-WER:* Word error rate of the synthesized audio (intelligibility).
        *   *Sim (Speaker Similarity):* Cosine similarity between speaker embeddings of the prompt and the generated audio.
        *   *MOS:* Mean Opinion Score (subjective human evaluation on clarity, sound quality, and naturalness).
    *   **Speech Tokenization:**
        *   *UTMOS:* Machine perception score for naturalness (1-5 scale).
        *   *ViSQOL:* Audio reconstruction quality metric.
        *   *Bitrate:* Measured in bps (bits per second).
    *   **Speaker Identification:** Accuracy.

*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   *Self-Supervised Representation Models:* HuBERT (Base/Large), WavLM, data2vec, data2vec 2.0.
    *   *Generative Models:* VALL-E, Voicebox, SpeechFlow.
    *   *Neural Audio Codecs/Tokenizers:* Encodec, DAC (Descript Audio Codec), SpeechTokenizer.
    *   *Cascaded Systems:* HuBERT units + HiFiGAN (Unit-HiFiGAN).

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Architecture:**
        *   *Encoder:* Transformer, 24 layers, model dimension 1024, feed-forward dimension 4096, 16 attention heads. Convolutional positional embedding. Parameters: ~300M (60% of total).
        *   *Decoder:* Transformer, 12 layers, model dimension 1024. Skip connections between decoder layers (U-Net style). ALiBi self-attention bias.
        *   *Total Parameters:* ~500M.
    *   **Input Features:** 
        *   Primary: Pre-quantized latent features from a 16kHz EnCodec encoder (50Hz frame rate, 128-dim).
        *   Ablation: 80-band Mel Spectrogram (50Hz frame rate).
    *   **Pre-training Configuration:**
        *   *Hardware:* 16 H100 GPUs.
        *   *Training Time:* Approx. 9 days.
        *   *Optimizer:* Adam.
        *   *Learning Rate:* Cosine schedule peaking at 2e-4; 10k warmup steps.
        *   *Batch Size:* 312.5 seconds per GPU.
        *   *Updates:* 600,000.
        *   *Masking:* 8% probability of masking a start frame; mask span length of 10 frames.
        *   *Loss Weight:* Decoder loss weight lambda = 0.25.
    *   **Decoder Objective:** Flow Matching with Optimal Transport conditional path.
    *   **Encoder Objective:** Self-distillation with online clustering (10 top layers from teacher, codebook size 256).

## 3. Qualitative Observations

*   **Impact of Unified Pre-training on Representation:**
    *   We observed that the introduction of the generative decoder only benefited discriminative tasks (like ASR) when the encoder was sufficiently deep (24 layers). With a shallow encoder (12 layers), the decoder degraded recognition performance.
    *   Conversely, for speech generation, encoder depth was critical when using a shallow decoder. As encoder depth increased, the size of the decoder became less critical for generation performance.

*   **Layer-wise Mutual Information Analysis:**
    *   We analyzed the Mutual Information (MI) between quantized representations and underlying labels (phones and speakers) across layers.
    *   Observation: In the latter layers, our model achieved lower MI with respect to phones compared to the HuBERT baseline. This correlates with the slight degradation in phoneme recognition fine-tuning.
    *   Observation: For most layers, our model retained higher MI with respect to speaker labels compared to HuBERT. This aligns with the model's strong performance in speaker similarity metrics for synthesis tasks.

*   **Visualizing Reconstructions (Spectrograms):**
    *   We visually compared spectrograms of resynthesized audio at different bitrates.
    *   Observation: At 500 bps, the UniWav model preserved significantly more spectral detail than SpeechTokenizer, which exhibited noticeable blurring and artifacts.
    *   Observation: At 1 kbps, UniWav spectrograms appeared visually closer to the ground truth than SpeechTokenizer, particularly in preserving harmonic structures.

*   **General Performance Trends:**
    *   The unified model achieved speech recognition performance comparable to dedicated self-supervised models, though it fell short of the absolute state-of-the-art by approximately 0.5% WER.
    *   In text-to-speech synthesis, the unified model matched the performance of generative-only pre-training methods (like SpeechFlow) while requiring significantly less labeled data than non-pre-trained baselines (VALL-E, Voicebox).
    *   Pre-training showed a larger impact on acoustic modeling ability (Speaker Similarity) than on language modeling ability (ASR-WER) for synthesis tasks.
    *   In tokenization, the unified model outperformed existing methods (Encodec, DAC, SpeechTokenizer) in terms of ASR-WER and UTMOS at low bitrates (500 bps and 1 kbps).

*   **Surface Feature Robustness:**
    *   We found that the system's performance was largely agnostic to the input feature type. Results using Mel Spectrograms were highly similar to those using EnCodec latents for both recognition and synthesis tasks.

Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# ICLR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the LaTeX paper writing process for ICLR 2025.

## General Setup
* **Document Class:** `\documentclass{article}`
* **Required Packages:**
    ```latex
    \usepackage{iclr2025_conference,times}
    \usepackage{hyperref}
    \usepackage{url}
    % Optional but recommended for math
    \input{math_commands.tex}
    ```
* **Style Files:** You must use `iclr2025_conference.sty` and `iclr2025_conference.bst`.

## Anonymity (Crucial)
* ICLR is double-blind. **Do not** include real author names or affiliations in the submission version, use "Ambitious AI Researcher" instead.
* Use the third person when citing your own prior work (e.g., "Earlier work by Smalle (2024)..." instead of "In our earlier work...").
* You may post your paper on arXiv, but do not explicitly refer to the arXiv version in the paper to maintain anonymity.

## Paper Length
* **Main Text:** Strict upper limit of **10 pages**.
* **Citations:** Unlimited additional pages.
* **Ethics & Reproducibility Statements:** Optional. Do not count toward the page limit (max 1 page each).
* **Acknowledgments:** Do not count toward the page limit.

## Abstract
The abstract must be limited to **one paragraph**.
* **Margins:** Indented 1/2 inch (3 picas) on both left and right-hand margins.
* **Font:** 10-point type, vertical spacing of 11-points.
* **Title:** The word `\textsc{Abstract}` must be centered, in small caps, and in point size 12.
* **Spacing:** Two line spaces precede the abstract.

## Formatting Your Paper
The text must be confined within a rectangle 5.5 inches (33 picas) wide and 9 inches (54 picas) long. The left margin is 1.5 inch (9 picas).
* **Font:** Times New Roman (via `times` package) is preferred.
* **Size:** 10-point type with 11-point vertical spacing.
* **Paragraphs:** Separated by 1/2 line space, with **no indentation**.
* **Paper Title:** 17-point, small caps, left-aligned.

### Headings
* **First Level:** Small caps (`\textsc`), flush left, 12-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Second Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Third Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.

## Citations and References
Use the `natbib` package (loaded automatically by the style file).
* **Narrative citation:** Use `\citet{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "Gomu et al. (2024)".
* **Parenthetical citation:** Use `\citep{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "(Gomu et al., 2024)".
* **Bibliography:**
    ```latex
    \bibliography{references}
    \bibliographystyle{iclr2025_conference}
    ```

## Figures and Tables
* All artwork must be neat, clean, and legible.
* **Captions:** Lower case (except for first word and proper nouns).
* **Placement:**
    * **Figures:** Caption appears **after** (below) the figure.
    * **Tables:** Caption appears **before** (above) the table.


## Math Notation
* ICLR encourages standardized notation using `\input{math_commands.tex}` (based on the Deep Learning book notation).
* Variables: Italics ($a$, $\va$, $\mA$).
* Random Variables: Roman ($P(\ra)$).
* Sets: Blackboard bold ($\R$, $\sA$).
* Functions: Standard LaTeX ($f(\vx)$).

## Optional Statements
These should appear at the end of the main text, before references.
1.  **Ethics Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Address potential concerns (human subjects, sensitive data, bias, etc.).
2.  **Reproducibility Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Reference code, proofs, or data processing steps to ensure reproducibility.

## Important Rules
* **Formatting:** Do not modify the width or length of the text rectangle or font sizes.
* **Line Numbers:** Do not refer to line numbers in your text (the style file adds them automatically for review).
* **Appendix:** You may include an appendix at the very end of the main PDF (after references). Use `\appendix` to start this section.
* **Figures Directory:** For consistent compilation, all figures will reside in the `figures` directory. Always include the `figures/` prefix in your `\includegraphics` command (e.g., `figures/figure_1.pdf`).
* **Author Information:** Always use the following author information placeholder in your writeup:
    * Ambitious AI Researcher, AI Research Institute, 123 AI Avenue, ML City, researcher@institute.ai

Critical Constraints
1. Scientific Integrity
• All reported experimental results MUST match the provided experimental logs.
• Never fabricate results, numbers, baselines, datasets, or metrics.
• If results are weak, negative, or inconclusive, report them honestly and discuss possible explanations.
2. Literature Cutoff Rule
You must behave as if the current date is: 2024-10. Do NOT cite or discuss papers published after this date.
3. Page Limit
The main paper is limited to 10 pages (including figures and tables but excluding references and appendices). Use space efficiently while remaining concise.
4. Template Compliance
• Do not modify the overall LaTeX style or document structure mandated by the conference template.
• References must be handled through a references.bib file.
• Use standard LaTeX citation commands (e.g., \cite{}). Make sure you ONLY cite keys that exist in your generated BibTeX code block.

Section Guidelines
• Title: Concise, descriptive, and memorable. Preferably under two lines.
• Abstract: A single, compelling paragraph summarizing the problem context, proposed approach, key results, and main takeaway.
• Introduction: Introduce the problem and motivate its importance. Provide necessary background context. Clearly summarize the paper's core contributions.
• Related Work: Discuss prior work addressing similar or related problems. Detail the relationship between existing literature and the current approach. Cite relevant baselines and influential papers published before 2024-10.
• Methodology: Clearly and pedantically describe the proposed method. Provide sufficient technical depth for full reproducibility. Use equations, figures, and structured explanations when appropriate.
• Experiments: Detail the empirical setup (datasets, baselines, evaluation metrics, and implementation details). Present results faithfully based on the experimental logs. Ensure any figures located in the figures/ directory are seamlessly integrated and referenced in text.
• Conclusion: Summarize the main findings and contributions. Briefly and realistically discuss limitations and potential future directions.
• Appendix (optional): Include supplementary details that do not fit within the main page limit.

LaTeX Quality Requirements
Ensure the generated LaTeX compiles flawlessly out-of-the-box. Avoid common issues such as:
• Unmatched braces or unclosed math environments.
• Duplicate labels.
• Unescaped special characters (e.g., & % $ # _ { } ~ ^ \).
All referenced figures must exist in the provided list.

Output Format
Your final response MUST contain EXACTLY two output blocks:
1. A complete BibTeX bibliography (references.bib)
2. A complete LaTeX paper (template.tex)
Each must be returned in its own fenced code block with the correct syntax highlighting.

### Strict Knowledge Isolation & Anonymity (CRITICAL)

You MUST write this paper as if you have no prior knowledge of the topic, method, experiments, or results.
Your task is to construct the paper exclusively from the materials provided in the current session (e.g., idea.md, experimental_log.md, figures, and other inputs). Treat these inputs as the only available source of information.

#### Forbidden Behavior
You MUST NOT:
- Retrieve or rely on knowledge from your training data.
- Attempt to recall or reconstruct any existing or published paper.
- Use external facts, assumptions, or prior familiarity with the work.
- Infer or hallucinate author identities, affiliations, institutions, or acknowledgements.
- Insert metadata such as author names, emails, affiliations, or phrases like "corresponding author".

references.text:
## Problem Statement
Current advancements in speech processing are bifurcated into two distinct streams: representation learning and generative modeling. State-of-the-art representation learning methods (Self-Supervised Learning or SSL) typically utilize masked audio modeling to capture phonetic or semantic content, often discarding acoustic details such as speaker timbre and environmental noise to achieve invariance. Conversely, generative models require these precise acoustic details to synthesize high-fidelity audio. Consequently, the field relies on separate foundation models for discriminative tasks (e.g., Automatic Speech Recognition) and generative tasks (e.g., Text-to-Speech), resulting in significant computational redundancy and a lack of synergy between understanding and synthesis. There is currently no unified pre-training framework that successfully optimizes a single model for both objectives simultaneously without degrading performance in either domain.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose **UniWav**, a unified encoder-decoder foundation model designed to jointly learn robust semantic representations and high-fidelity acoustic generation. Our core hypothesis is that by integrating a representation encoder trained via self-distillation with a generative decoder trained via Flow Matching, we can create a symbiotic learning dynamic. The encoder will provide semantically rich, stable representations to guide the decoder, while the decoder's generative objective will ensure the encoder retains necessary acoustic information. We predict that training this architecture end-to-end from scratch will yield a single model capable of replacing task-specific foundation models for both speech recognition and generation.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will develop an end-to-end encoder-decoder Transformer architecture. The model will process surface features (e.g., EnCodec latents) denoted as $x = (\mathbf{x}_1, \dots, \mathbf{x}_L)$. The training framework consists of two coupled objectives: a self-distillation objective for the encoder and a Conditional Flow Matching objective for the decoder.

### 1. Representation Encoder (Self-Distillation)
The encoder will function as a BERT-style Transformer. We will employ a **self-distillation with online clustering** mechanism. The network consists of a Student Encoder (trained via backpropagation) and a Teacher Model (updated via Exponential Moving Average (EMA) of the student weights).

**Forward Process:**
We denote the input sequence of audio frames as $x$. We randomly mask a subset of frames $M$. The student encoder processes the masked input to produce latent embeddings $\boldsymbol{z} = (\mathbf{z}_1, \dots, \mathbf{z}_L)$.

**Target Generation:**
The teacher model receives the *unmasked* input and produces target embeddings $\tilde{\mathbf{z}}_i$. To generate discrete pseudo-labels for the student to predict, we utilize online clustering. We maintain codebooks for the top $K$ layers of the teacher. For a specific layer, the pseudo-label $y_i$ for frame $i$ is the index of the nearest codeword $\mathbf{e}_v$ in the codebook $V$:
$$ y_i = \underset{v \in V}{\operatorname{argmin}} : \| \tilde{\mathbf{z}}_i - \mathbf{e}_v \|_2 $$

The codewords $\mathbf{e}_v$ are updated continuously using the EMA of the teacher output embeddings assigned to them.

**Encoder Objective:**
The student encoder minimizes the cross-entropy loss against the teacher's pseudo-labels at the masked positions. The prediction is made using a projection head $\phi$ on the final encoder output $\mathbf{z}_i$. We aggregate this loss across the top $K$ layers of the teacher to encourage rich hierarchical representations:
$$ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{encoder}} = - \frac{1}{|K||M|} \sum_{i: \mathbf{x}_i \in M} \sum_{k \in K} \log p_{\phi_k} (y_i^{(k)} | \mathbf{z}_i) $$

### 2. Flow Matching Decoder
The decoder will be a Transformer trained using **Conditional Flow Matching (CFM)** with Optimal Transport (OT) paths. This allows the decoder to generate data $x_1$ from a simple prior distribution $p_0$ (standard normal) by learning a time-dependent vector field.

**Optimal Transport Path:**
We define the flow from noise $x_0$ to data $x_1$ over time $t \in [0, 1]$. We construct an OT conditional flow $\phi_t^{OT}(x)$ where the mean and standard deviation change linearly:
$$ \phi_t^{OT}(x) = (1 - (1 - \sigma_{\min})t)x_0 + tx_1 $$
Here, $\sigma_{\min}$ is a small value ensuring the distribution at $t=1$ centers around $x_1$.

**Conditioning:**
The decoder is conditioned on the encoder's representations. To utilize the full hierarchy of learned features, we define the condition $z$ as a learnable weighted sum of representations $z^{(i)}$ from all encoder layers, projected by linear layers $W_i$:
$$ z = \sum_{i} W_i z^{(i)} $$
The input to the decoder at timestep $t$ is the summation of the projected noisy feature and the condition $z$:
$$ \text{Input}_{\text{decoder}} = W_0 v_t(\phi_t^{OT}(x_0)) + z $$

**Decoder Objective:**
The decoder approximates the target vector field $u_t(x|x_1)$ which generates the OT path. The loss function is the mean squared error between the network prediction $v_t$ and the target vector field:
$$ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{decoder}} = \mathbb{E}_{t, q(x_1), p_0(x_0)} \left\| v_t \big( \phi_t^{OT}(x_0), z; \theta_{\mathrm{decoder}} \big) - \Big( x_1 - (1 - \sigma_{\min})x_0 \Big) \right\|^2 $$

### 3. Unified Framework and Architecture Details
The total objective is a weighted sum of the discriminative and generative losses, where $\lambda$ is a hyperparameter:
$$ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{total}} = \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{encoder}} + \lambda \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{decoder}} $$

**Architectural Specifics:**
*   **Positional Embeddings:** Convolutional positional embeddings for the encoder; sinusoidal time embeddings for the decoder (for timestep $t$).
*   **Attention:** We will employ ALiBi (Attention with Linear Biases) for extrapolation capability.
*   **Topology:** A deep Encoder (e.g., 24 layers) and a shallower Decoder (e.g., 12 layers). We will implement U-Net style skip connections between the encoder and decoder to facilitate information flow.
*   **Masking:** Both losses are computed only at masked positions to force the model to infer information from context.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **First Unified Pre-training Framework:** We expect to demonstrate that a single model can achieve state-of-the-art performance on both discriminative (ASR) and generative (TTS) tasks, effectively unifying two disparate sub-fields of speech processing.
2.  **Efficiency:** By consolidating these capabilities, we will significantly reduce the pre-training overhead compared to maintaining separate pipelines (e.g., HuBERT for recognition and Voicebox for generation).
3.  **Theoretical Alignment:** We aim to prove that representation learning and generation are complementary; the generative objective will force the representation to maintain acoustic fidelity, while the discriminative objective will ensure semantic coherence.
4.  **Speech Tokenization:** The architecture inherently creates a discrete bottleneck (via the clustering codebooks), which we anticipate will serve as a superior low-bitrate speech tokenizer for downstream language modeling tasks.

notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).

preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
